'''Sophie Piccard''' (1904–1990) was a Russian-Swiss mathematician who became the first female full professor (professor ordinarius) in Switzerland.<ref name="asc"/><ref name="hds"/> Her research concerned [[set theory]], [[group theory]], [[linear algebra]], and the [[history of mathematics]].<ref name="asc">{{citation|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/piccard.htm|title=Sophie Piccard|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]]|date=January 10, 2014|first=Larry|last=Riddle}}.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Piccard was born on September 27, 1904, in [[Saint Petersburg]], with a French [[Huguenot]] mother and a Swiss father. She earned a diploma in [[Smolensk]] in 1925, where her father, Eugène-Ferdinand Piccard, was a university professor and her mother a language teacher at the lycée. Soon afterwards she moved to Switzerland with her parents, escaping the unrest in Russia that her mother, [[Eulalie Piccard]], would become known for writing about. Sophie Piccard's Russian degree was worthless in Switzerland, and she earned another from the [[University of Lausanne]] in 1927, going on to complete a doctorate there in 1929 under the supervision of [[Dmitry Mirimanoff]].<ref name="asc"/><ref name="hds"/><ref name="bdws"/>

==Career and later life==
She worked outside of mathematics until 1936, when she began teaching part-time at the [[University of Neuchâtel]] as an assistant to Rudolf Gaberel. Gaberel died in 1938 and she inherited his position, becoming a professor extraordinarius (associate professor). She was promoted to professor ordinarius in 1943, as the chair of higher geometry and probability theory at Neuchâtel.<ref name="asc"/><ref name="hds">{{citation|contribution-url=http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/d/D45160.php|contribution=Piccard, Sophie|title=Historical Dictionary of Switzerland|first=Sandrine|last=Zaslavsky|date=February 1, 2010|title-link=Historical Dictionary of Switzerland}}.</ref><ref name="bdws">{{citation|title=The Biographical Dictionary of Women in Science: Pioneering Lives from Ancient Times to the Mid-20th Century, Vol. 2: L-Z|first1=Marilyn Bailey|last1=Ogilvie|first2=Joy Dorothy|last2=Harvey|author-link=Marilyn Bailey Ogilvie|author2-link=Joy Harvey|publisher=Taylor & Francis|year=2000|isbn=9780415920407|contribution=Piccard, Sophie (ca. 1906– )|pages=1019–1020|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LTSYePZvSXYC&pg=PA1019}}.</ref>

Piccard died on January 6, 1990, in [[Fribourg]].<ref name="asc"/>

==Contributions==
Piccard was an [[list of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1932 and again in 1936.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.mathunion.org/db/ICM/Speakers/SortedByLastname.php|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers since 1897|publisher=[[International Mathematical Union]]|accessdate=2015-10-02}}.</ref>

In 1939 she published the book ''Sur les ensembles de distances des ensembles de points d'un espace Euclidien'' (''Mémoires de L’Université de Neuchâtel'' 13, Paris, France: Libraire Gauthier-Villars and Cie., 1939).<ref name="asc"/><ref>{{citation|last=Ficken|first=F. A.|title=Review: Sophie Piccard, Sur les ensembles de distances des ensembles de points d'un espace Euclidien|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=49|year=1943|issue=1|pages=29–31|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183504924|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1943-07825-1|doi-access=free}}.</ref> Its subject was the sets of distances that a collection of points in a [[Euclidean space]] might determine.
This book included early research on [[Golomb ruler]]s, finite sets of integer points in a one-dimensional space with the property that their distances are all distinct.
She published a theorem claiming that every two Golomb rulers with the same [[distance set]] must be congruent to each other; this turned out to be false for certain sets of six points, but true otherwise.<ref>{{citation
